question: What is the time frame for defining puerperal sepsis following childbirth?

options.A: Strictly during the active stage of labor
options.D: Only during the first 24 hours postpartum

explanation: Puerperal sepsis is officially defined as an infection of the genital tract occurring anytime from the onset of membrane rupture or labor up to 42 days following delivery. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T024#GNS226_U3_T024_h1)

question: Why must a nurse catch postpartum infections early?

options.A: Postpartum infections can quickly escalate into systemic illness and shock
options.B: It guarantees the patient will not need any form of surgical intervention
options.C: Delayed involution of the uterus is the only complication that ever occurs
options.D: Routine hospital discharge protocols require a confirmed negative blood culture

explanation: Spotting an infection early makes a huge difference! A localized postpartum infection can quickly turn into severe sepsis if we don't catch and treat it promptly. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T024#GNS226_U3_T024_h1)

question: Which bacteria is well-known for causing rapid and severe postpartum infections?
explanation: Group A Streptococcus is notorious in midwifery for causing very rapid and severe illness in new mothers. Quick action is always key here! [learn more](GNS226_U3_T024#GNS226_U3_T024_h2)

question: Why is the postpartum uterine cavity so easily invaded by bacteria?

options.A: Gastric acid production increases significantly during labor
options.B: The cervix remains completely dilated for several months
options.C: Normal flora inside the uterus becomes entirely pathogenic
options.D: The placental site is a large, raw, vascular wound

explanation: Think of where the placenta detached—it leaves behind a large, healing wound with open blood vessels. This makes it a very easy pathway for bacteria to enter. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T024#GNS226_U3_T024_h2)

question: Which of the following is a major risk factor for puerperal sepsis?
explanation: When membranes rupture for a long time before delivery, bacteria have a direct open pathway to travel up into the uterus. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T024#GNS226_U3_T024_h3)

question: Why does an emergency cesarean delivery carry a higher infection risk than a planned vaginal birth?

options.A: Patients undergoing cesarean birth never receive prophylactic antibiotics
options.B: Surgical incision exposes internal tissues and prior labor introduces bacteria
options.C: Suturing techniques used in emergency surgery always trap skin flora
options.D: The sterile operating theatre environment promotes bacterial growth

explanation: An abdominal surgery creates a fresh wound, and if the mother was already in labor with ruptured membranes, bacteria may have already entered the lower reproductive tract. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T024#GNS226_U3_T024_h3)

question: What is usually the very first sign of puerperal sepsis in a new mother?
explanation: Always watch out for temperature spikes! A sudden fever is typically the earliest and most important warning sign that an infection is brewing postpartum. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T024#GNS226_U3_T024_h4)

question: How does the uterus typically feel when assessing a patient with puerperal sepsis?

options.A: Soft, boggy, tender, and larger than expected for the postpartum day
options.B: Displaced entirely to the left side with no tenderness
options.C: Firm, contracted, non-tender, and well below the umbilicus
options.D: Completely rigid like a board with absent bowel sounds

explanation: Infection slows down normal uterine shrinking (involution). Instead of feeling firm, a septic uterus often feels soft, bulky, and painful when you touch it. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T024#GNS226_U3_T024_h4)

question: Why must blood cultures be drawn before giving the first dose of antibiotics?

options.A: Antibiotic molecules interfere with the chemical reagents used in the laboratory
options.B: Antibiotics can kill the bacteria in the blood sample and cause a false-negative result
options.C: Laboratory policy strictly forbids drawing blood after medication administration
options.D: Blood pressure drops too quickly once antibiotics enter the bloodstream

explanation: We need to catch the germ alive! If we give antibiotics first, they might kill the bacteria in our blood sample, making the lab test look normal when the patient is actually still sick. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T024#GNS226_U3_T024_h5)

question: Which imaging tool is best used to check for retained pieces of the placenta when sepsis is suspected?
explanation: A pelvic ultrasound is safe, quick, and helps us peek inside the uterus to see if any placental tissue was left behind. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T024#GNS226_U3_T024_h5)

question: Why are broad-spectrum antibiotics started immediately instead of waiting for lab results?

options.A: Culture results are always inaccurate during the postpartum period
options.B: Delaying treatment allows the infection to worsen rapidly and threaten life
options.C: Broad-spectrum drugs have no side effects for the nursing mother
options.D: Hospital accreditation standards fine units that delay medication

explanation: Sepsis is a race against time! Waiting days for lab results could let the infection spiral out of control, so we start treatment right away. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T024#GNS226_U3_T024_h6)

question: What procedure is often needed if leftover placental tissue is causing ongoing postpartum sepsis?
explanation: If dead placental tissue is trapped inside, antibiotics alone won't clear it. We need to gently clear out the uterus to help the mother heal. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T024#GNS226_U3_T024_h6)

question: Why is closely monitoring urine output so crucial for a patient with sepsis?

options.A: It proves that the patient is drinking enough oral fluids
options.B: It is a reliable indicator of adequate kidney perfusion and fluid status
options.C: It prevents the bladder from becoming distended during sleep
options.D: It eliminates the need to check blood pressure every hour

explanation: Urine output is our window into how well the kidneys and vital organs are getting blood flow. Good urine output means the body is holding up against shock! [learn more](GNS226_U3_T024#GNS226_U3_T024_h7)

question: What is the most important infection control practice for nurses doing perineal care or dressing changes?

options.A: Using scented antiseptic soaps for all skin surfaces
options.B: Wearing sterile gowns for routine temperature checks
options.C: Isolating the mother from her newborn baby
options.D: Rigorous hand hygiene and aseptic technique

explanation: Simple hand hygiene and clean sterile technique are your absolute best defenses against bringing new germs into healing wounds. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T024#GNS226_U3_T024_h7)

question: What is the major danger of failing to treat puerperal sepsis promptly?

options.A: Immediate closure of the fallopian tubes
options.C: Permanent discoloration of the skin and hair
options.D: Progression to septic shock and multi-organ failure

explanation: An infection left unchecked in the uterus won't just stay there—it can spread through the whole body, causing a dangerous drop in blood pressure and organ failure. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T024#GNS226_U3_T024_h8)

question: Which of the following is an effective way to help prevent puerperal sepsis during labor?

options.A: Delaying bladder emptying until after delivery
options.B: Encouraging strict bed rest for the entire duration of labor
options.C: Limiting the number of unnecessary vaginal examinations
options.D: Avoiding all routine perineal hygiene measures

explanation: Every vaginal exam is a chance to introduce bacteria. Doing only necessary exams helps keep the birth canal safer from outside germs. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T024#GNS226_U3_T024_h8)
